items.stem: In the rumour, who would bow down before Gotama and become his students?
items.quote: He was said to wander through the land, teaching, surrounded by disciples, without possession, without home, without a wife, in the yellow cloak of an ascetic, but with a cheerful brow, a man of bliss, and Brahmins and princes would bow down before him and would become his students.
items.why: The rumour says even the highest ranks honour Gotama.

items.stem: Who spoke of the legend of Gotama in the forest?
items.quote: This myth, this rumour, this legend resounded, its fragrants rose up, here and there; in the towns, the Brahmins spoke of it and in the forest, the Samanas; again and again, the name of Gotama, the Buddha reached the ears of the young men, with good and with bad talk, with praise and with defamation.
items.why: The legend reaches even the forest where the friends live.

items.stem: Who suggests that the friends go to hear the Buddha?
items.quote: Speak, friend, wouldn’t we want to go there too and listen to the teachings from the Buddha’s mouth?”
items.why: The suggestion to go comes from Govinda.

items.stem: Siddhartha leaves the Samanas without telling the oldest one.
items.quote: On this very same day, Siddhartha informed the oldest one of the Samanas of his decision, that he wanted to leave him.
items.why: He tells the oldest Samana of his decision that same day.

items.stem: Siddhartha is the one who asks, “How do you think, Govinda?”
items.quote: “How do you think, Govinda,”
items.why: Siddhartha opens the friends' talk about their progress.

items.stem: Complete: “long nails grew slowly on his ____ fingers”
items.quote: Feverish dreams flickered from his enlarged eyes, long nails grew slowly on his parched fingers and a dry, shaggy beard grew on his chin.
items.why: The detail shows how his body changes in the forest.

items.stem: To whom does Siddhartha leave feats like walking on water?
items.quote: Let old Samanas be content with such feats!
items.why: He wants no part of such feats.

items.stem: Govinda guesses the oldest Samana is about sixty years old.
items.quote: Our oldest one might be about sixty years of age.
items.why: Govinda gives the old man's age.

items.stem: Siddhartha's soul slips inside a dead tiger on the riverbank.
items.quote: A dead jackal was lying on the sandy bank
items.why: It is a dead jackal, not a tiger.

items.stem: Match each animal to what it does.
items.why: In meditation his soul enters animals.
evidence: A heron flew over the bamboo forest
A dead jackal was lying on the sandy bank

items.stem: Which wonder was reported of Gotama?
items.quote: Many wonderful and unbelievable things were reported of him, he had performed miracles, had overcome the devil, had spoken to the gods.
items.why: Wonders are part of the story told about him.

items.stem: Believers said Gotama was never again submerged in what?
items.quote: He possessed, so the believers said, the highest enlightenment, he remembered his previous lives, he had reached the nirvana and never returned into the cycle, was never again submerged in the murky river of physical forms.
items.why: The believers' report uses a striking image.

items.stem: Govinda stops on the path and raises his hands before he answers.
items.quote: At this, Govinda stopped on the path, rose his hands, and spoke: “If you, Siddhartha, only would not bother your friend with this kind of talk!
items.why: Govinda halts mid-walk to answer his friend.

items.stem: Siddhartha speaks these doubts while sitting alone in meditation.
items.quote: And once again, another time, when Siddhartha left the forest together with Govinda, to beg for some food in the village for their brothers and teachers, Siddhartha began to speak and said: “What now, O Govinda, might we be on the right path?
items.why: He speaks them aloud to Govinda as they walk from the forest.

items.stem: Match each group to what it says or does about Gotama.
items.why: Different groups react to the news in different ways.
evidence: He possessed, so the believers said, the highest enlightenment, he remembered his previous lives, he had reached the nirvana and never returned into the cycle, was never again submerged in the murky river of physical forms.
But his enemies and disbelievers said, this Gotama was a vain seducer, he would spent his days in luxury, scorned the offerings, was without learning, and knew neither exercises nor self-castigation.

This myth, this rumour, this legend resounded, its fragrants rose up, here and there; in the towns, the Brahmins spoke of it and in the forest, the Samanas; again and again, the name of Gotama, the Buddha reached the ears of the young men, with good and with bad talk, with praise and with defamation.

items.stem: Put these events in story order.
items.why: The news of Gotama leads straight to the friends' leaving.
evidence: He was said to wander through the land, teaching, surrounded by disciples, without possession, without home, without a wife, in the yellow cloak of an ascetic, but with a cheerful brow, a man of bliss, and Brahmins and princes would bow down before him and would become his students.

On this very same day, Siddhartha informed the oldest one of the Samanas of his decision, that he wanted to leave him.
Govinda was startled and became embarrassed.

items.stem: What did Siddhartha give to a poor Brahmin?
items.quote: Siddhartha gave his garments to a poor Brahmin in the street.
items.why: He gives up his clothes at the start.

items.stem: Complete: “the circle is a ____, we have already ascended many a level.”
items.quote: the circle is a spiral, we have already ascended many a level.
items.why: Govinda pictures their path as climbing.

items.stem: In Siddhartha's comparison, where does the oxcart driver find numbing?
items.quote: what the driver of an oxcart finds in the inn
items.why: He likens the exercises to a driver's drinking.

items.stem: Put the friends' first talk in order.
items.why: Govinda's praise meets Siddhartha's doubt.

cards.text: Govinda: a Samana isn't a drunkard

evidence: how do you think did we progress?
One day, you’ll be a holy man, O Siddhartha.
In every tavern of that part of a town

items.stem: Why was every pilgrim welcome among the Brahmins' sons?
items.quote: Everywhere where the rumour of Buddha was heard, everywhere in the lands of India, the young men listened up, felt a longing, felt hope, and among the Brahmins’ sons of the towns and villages every pilgrim and stranger was welcome, when he brought news of him, the exalted one, the Sakyamuni.
items.why: News of Gotama is what the young men are hungry for.

items.stem: Why does Gotama's name keep reaching the young men in the forest?
items.quote: This myth, this rumour, this legend resounded, its fragrants rose up, here and there; in the towns, the Brahmins spoke of it and in the forest, the Samanas; again and again, the name of Gotama, the Buddha reached the ears of the young men, with good and with bad talk, with praise and with defamation.
items.why: Talk in both towns and forest carries the name to them.

items.stem: Why does Govinda feel embarrassed as they take their leave?
items.quote: Govinda was startled and became embarrassed.
items.why: The oldest Samana's angry reaction makes the leave-taking awkward.

items.stem: Govinda asks Siddhartha not to bother his friend with such talk.
items.quote: At this, Govinda stopped on the path, rose his hands, and spoke: “If you, Siddhartha, only would not bother your friend with this kind of talk!
items.why: Govinda wants the conversation to stop.

items.stem: Govinda calls the words “terrible” because he agrees with Siddhartha.
items.quote: spoke Govinda, “wouldn’t speak such terrible words, Siddhartha!
items.why: He calls them terrible because he cannot accept them.

items.stem: The rumour calls Gotama “a man of ____”
items.quote: He was said to wander through the land, teaching, surrounded by disciples, without possession, without home, without a wife, in the yellow cloak of an ascetic, but with a cheerful brow, a man of bliss, and Brahmins and princes would bow down before him and would become his students.
items.why: A joyful, blissful figure is part of what draws seekers to the story.

items.stem: Why do the friends rarely talk about the myth?
items.quote: They rarely talked about it, because the oldest one of the Samanas did not like this myth.
items.why: The oldest Samana's dislike keeps them quiet.

items.stem: What does Siddhartha whisper that he wants to show the old man?
items.quote: “Now, I want to show the old man that I’ve learned something from him.”
items.why: He means to prove what the Samanas taught him.

items.stem: Siddhartha stays silent because he is thinking Govinda's words through.
items.quote: He thought about the words which Govinda had said to him and thought the words through to their end.
items.why: He weighs his friend's words fully.

items.stem: Govinda thinks casting a spell on an old Samana is easy.
items.quote: It is hard, it is very hard to cast a spell on an old Samana.
items.why: Govinda is impressed because it is very hard.

items.stem: What does the triple “This myth, this rumour, this legend” chiefly suggest?
items.quote: This myth, this rumour, this legend resounded, its fragrants rose up, here and there; in the towns, the Brahmins spoke of it and in the forest, the Samanas; again and again, the name of Gotama, the Buddha reached the ears of the young men, with good and with bad talk, with praise and with defamation.
items.why: Each new name for the story makes it sound larger.

items.stem: “On this very same day” chiefly stresses Siddhartha's what?
items.quote: On this very same day, Siddhartha informed the oldest one of the Samanas of his decision, that he wanted to leave him.
items.why: He acts on his choice without delay.

items.stem: In the believers' account, what does “the murky river of physical forms” stand for?
items.quote: He possessed, so the believers said, the highest enlightenment, he remembered his previous lives, he had reached the nirvana and never returned into the cycle, was never again submerged in the murky river of physical forms.
items.why: The image pictures bodily existence as something one can sink in.

items.stem: The enemies' charge that Gotama “knew neither exercises nor self-castigation” judges him by the Samanas' own standards.
items.quote: But his enemies and disbelievers said, this Gotama was a vain seducer, he would spent his days in luxury, scorned the offerings, was without learning, and knew neither exercises nor self-castigation.
items.why: Their complaint counts as faults the very practices the Samanas value.

items.stem: Siddhartha's question “might we be on the right path?” shows he is sure the Samanas' way is right.
items.quote: And once again, another time, when Siddhartha left the forest together with Govinda, to beg for some food in the village for their brothers and teachers, Siddhartha began to speak and said: “What now, O Govinda, might we be on the right path?
items.why: A question like this voices doubt, not certainty.

items.stem: Complete: “its ____ rose up, here and there”
items.quote: This myth, this rumour, this legend resounded, its fragrants rose up, here and there; in the towns, the Brahmins spoke of it and in the forest, the Samanas; again and again, the name of Gotama, the Buddha reached the ears of the young men, with good and with bad talk, with praise and with defamation.
items.why: The rumour is pictured as a scent drifting through the land.

items.stem: What does Siddhartha's phrase “the agony of being a self” imply?
items.quote: a short escape of the agony of being a self
items.why: He feels selfhood itself as pain.

items.stem: Siddhartha says, “I am willing to listen to these teachings.” This comes despite what?
items.quote: I have grown distrustful and tired against teachings and learning
items.why: He agrees to go while doubting teachings.

items.stem: Complete: “just as far removed from wisdom, from salvation, as a child in the mother’s ____”
items.quote: as a child in the mother’s womb
items.why: The simile puts him at the very beginning, not near wisdom.

items.stem: Order the steps of Siddhartha's argument in ¶20.
items.why: From one old man he reasons to all Samanas.
